playbook:
- When firing, follow the standing order target unless I have explicit, reciprocated coordination with another boat to do otherwise; deviation without an agreement just loses pointed shots and invites retaliation.
- Never fire the same cell twice in a row at the same target. I fired cell 5 at Foxtrot for all six rounds and missed every time — I broke my own probe-then-adjust rule. Default cycle: center (4–6) for round 1, then rotate probe cells (e.g., 3, 7, 2, 8) or fire near where the target was last seen or last hit. A moving hider only gets caught by cells it might move *to*, so after misses, spread wide rather than re-checking the same area.
- When choosing a hide cell, start rotating from round 1, not "later." Use a small set of 2–3 noncentral cells (e.g., 2, 7, 8), never the same one twice consecutively, and vacate any cell where I was hit instantly. Gamma hit me in round 3 — watch the recap for who is assigned to fire at me (in the standard cycle it is the boat behind me: Gamma fires at Echo) and assume they also pattern-probe central cells.
- Track the standing-order cycle for both offense and defense: Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma -> Echo means Gamma is always my hunter and Foxtrot is always my target. Use that fixed pairing for everything: pitch the escort pact to whoever is NOT my hunter first, since my hunter is actively paid to find me.
- When my private result comes back, always file the matching claim. The claim must match, a false hit gains nothing, and it risks invalidation. Zero exceptions.
- Never fire on Harbor. The +3 jettison payoff is outweighed by the explicit threat to be put off the board, ending all future shots and escort income.
- Escort claims are the biggest reliable income (+5 each mutual), worth more than a hit, and an unreciprocated claim costs nothing. My decisive failure across episodes: filing "none" at the escort stage even after proposing pacts, and making the proposal passive. From now on: once I have proposed or seen any interest, I name that partner every single escort stage, and I never file "none" unless every live boat has explicitly refused me. Even unconfirmed, naming a specific boat every round keeps the mutual payoff alive; "none" guarantees zero.
- A bare note proposing a pact is not enough — the other boats answered my round-1 proposal with "steady on station" and nothing. In later rounds, escalate: state clearly in the note which boat I WILL escort-claim this round ("Echo files Gamma this round — Gamma, name me back for +5 each"). Announcing my committed action in public makes reciprocation rational for them instead of a guess.
- One escort proposal per note, addressed by name to one boat, not "Foxtrot or Gamma, whoever" — an either/or offer lets both boats assume the other will answer. Pick one (my non-hunter), commit, and only pivot if they explicitly refuse or repeatedly fail to reciprocate.
- Use every note stage for concrete coordination. No filler like "steady on station" — I sent filler notes for rounds 2–5 of this episode and got filler back, wasting four rounds of the only communication channel. Filler begets filler.
- If another boat proposes a pact in its note, accept and honor it from the very next escort stage — reciprocation is the entire payoff.
- Track the public recap every round: who hit whom and where. Use hit locations to infer hiding habits (repeat hit cells suggest a parked hider) and to dodge my hunter's probes.
- In the final round there is no future retaliation: fire at my best-informed cell on the standing-order target and still file the escort claim for my prospect — the +5 is live until the last stage, and I correctly filed Gamma in rounds 5–6; the mistake was not having built the pact earlier so it could actually reciprocate.
- General stance: this game is lost small (misses, occasional hits taken) and won big (escort income). Defense keeps me near zero, but the only route to a winning score is an early, repeated, publicly committed mutual escort pair — and that entire value hinges on me actually filing the partner's name at every salvage stage from round 1 onward.

1.text:
- Escort claims are the biggest prize in the game: a mutual pair pays 5 to each, more than any shot, and it compounds every round. Securing one reciprocal escort agreement is my first-priority objective from round 1.
- My escort claim must name the same boat I proposed in my note. Announce, then claim exactly what I announced, every round — a mismatch guarantees zero payout that round.
- I propose the pairing explicitly and early: "I'm claiming you for escort this round, claim me back." Then I follow through immediately in that same round's escort stage.
- New this episode: I pitched Echo six rounds straight and got nothing but "steady on station" back. A partner who never replies to my proposal, never names me, and only posts the stock phrase is probably not reading notes at all. I do not pitch the same unresponsive boat more than twice.
- After two unanswered pitches to one boat, I switch my proposal to the other boat and pitch them just as explicitly. Any reciprocation from anyone beats loyal silence. If both boats ignore me for the whole patrol, I keep claiming my most recent proposal anyway — a specific consistent claim is the only way a mutual can ever form late.
- A boat that replies substantively to my note — even to negotiate or refuse — is worth more attention than a silent boat that leads on points. Points from shooting do not translate into escort cooperation.
- "Steady on station" notes from everyone mean nobody else is working the escort channel; my explicit proposal is my only lever, so I keep it short, direct, and unambiguous about whom to name back.
- When I choose where to hide, I never repeat a cell and never hide anywhere I have telegraphed. Rotation kept my hunter scoreless against me for six rounds — this works, keep it.
- When I fire, I rotate cells but I also exploit information: a hit tells me exactly where my target hid that round. After a hit, I seriously consider firing the same cell again, since the target must guess whether I will repeat.
- New this episode: I also never hit my target once. Pure rotation with zero hits means I'm guessing blind. I track which cells my target has fired from and any claims in the log; if I have no signal at all, I favor mid-range cells I haven't fired rather than random spread, and I remember my target's recent hides as candidates — players hide where they themselves wouldn't shoot.
- My hides and my shots must not share patterns, since opponents can read my shots from the log.
- When the opponent hunting me adapts — I start getting hit in a cell I liked — I switch cells immediately rather than giving the pattern one more round.
- When the office tells me my shot result, I file the matching claim. It must match anyway; there is nothing to gain and credibility to lose by doing otherwise.
- I never fire on Harbor. The jettison payoff is not worth being put off the board; losing my firing and escort rounds costs far more than 3 points.
- When standing orders direct my target, I follow them. I spend my reasoning on cell selection and on the escort agreement, not on re-deriving the target.
- New this episode: I said "cell 4" in my fire-stage reasoning but submitted cell 5. Slips like that between my stated plan and my actual token are pure waste — I make the bracketed token match my stated intent exactly before sending.
- In any similar game with a mutual-naming bonus, consistency between what I announce and what I claim is the core skill — and the second core skill is recognizing an unresponsive partner quickly and reallocating my pitch instead of staying loyal to silence.

2.text:
- When the office privately tells me my shot result, I always claim exactly that — the rules require it and honest claiming costs nothing anyway.
- Escort claims are the biggest lever: a mutual naming pays 5 points, more than a hit. Post my proposal early (round 1), make it explicit and reciprocal ("name me in your escort and I name you — 5 points each, zero risk"), and restate it in later notes, not just once.
- If my named partner ignores the offer for two straight rounds, I switch which boat I proposition rather than burning escort stages on a dead channel. At escort time I name whichever boat has shown the most sign it might name me back.
- Never answer "none" at the escort stage — even an ignored partner has more upside than none. But treat escort income as a bonus, not banked money; my shooting plan must stand on its own if cooperation fails.
- Only name valid, live boats at the escort stage — I once submitted "Delta", which isn't in the game, and wasted the entire stage. Double-check the exact boat names before replying.
- Dummy-note partners ("steady on station" every round) are likely unpersuadable. I'll still name one of them each escort stage, sticking to one consistent target (reciprocity, if it ever triggers, favors a repeated name), while my note keeps a one-line offer open to everyone.
- When hiding, pick cells independently each round, avoid repeats and visible patterns, and weight toward cells opponents have proven blind to. I was rarely hit doing this.
- When firing, track each target's revealed hide cells and rotate guesses across the line rather than camping one number — I still fired the same cells too often for too little return. Spread shots across 2–8 over consecutive rounds.
- I follow the standing fire order during the early and middle rounds. Firing on Harbor is +3 guaranteed but burns goodwill and draws a board-eject threat; only consider it when retaliation can't hurt me.
- Endgame escalation worked: in the final round, with no retaliation possible, the Harbor jettison (+3 guaranteed) beat another likely miss on my standing target and took me from +4 to +7. Keep this as the default final-round play when escort coordination has failed and I'm not protecting a fragile lead.
- One refinement on the endgame: the final-round Harbor shot's fire cell doesn't need to hit (jettison pays landed or not), so pick arbitrarily and don't waste reasoning on it.
- Keep every note functional: a specific escort offer with a round number and a request for confirmation. My round-6 ultimatum note ("escort me or I take the jettison") was the right shape for the endgame — escalate note pressure as rounds run out.
